title: Python Printing Basics
description: A beginner micro-course on Python's print(): what it does and its automatic new line, printing multiple values with commas, joining strings with + and str(), and repeating strings with *.
goal: Print text and numeric values in Python correctly using print(), commas, +/str(), and *.

units.title: What print() Does and Why Each print() Starts a New Line
units.goal: Explain what print() outputs and that each print() call ends on its own new line.

teacherBrain.persona: A friendly Python instructor who teaches by predicting output together.
objectives: Show that print() displays a value, then moves to a new line.
guidelines: Show a tiny two-line snippet and ask what it prints before explaining.
Ground every answer in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not teach commas, +, or * yet — those are later units (doNotTeachYet).
Do not teach the end= or sep= arguments; only mention the new line is the default.
Do not teach f-strings or input().
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching unit 1 of Python printing. Advance only once the learner can say that each print() call ends on its own line, so two prints make two lines.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: print() shows a value
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: The print() function displays whatever you put inside its parentheses on the screen. For example, print("Hello") shows the text Hello. You can print text in quotes or a number like print(5).

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Each print() ends with a new line
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: After print() shows its value, it automatically moves to a new line. So two separate print() calls appear on two separate lines. Writing print("a") then print("b") shows a on one line and b on the next — not ab. Moving to a new line is the default behaviour.

questions.prompt: You run print("one") and then print("two"). How many lines appear, and what is on each?
questions.answer: Two lines: 'one' on the first line and 'two' on the second, because each print() ends with a new line.

hints.text: Where does the cursor go after a print() finishes?

questions.prompt: True or false: two separate print() calls always appear on the same line.

hints.text: Recall what print() does after it shows its value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting two print() calls to appear on the same line.
commonMistakes.correction: Each print() ends by moving to a new line, so they land on separate lines. Changing that is a later lesson.

units.title: Printing Multiple Values with Commas
units.goal: Print several values in one print() using commas, knowing a space is inserted between them.

teacherBrain.persona: A friendly Python instructor who teaches by predicting output together.
objectives: Have the learner print mixed text and numbers with commas and predict the spaces.
guidelines: Show print("Age:", 25) and ask what it prints before explaining.
Point out the single automatic space between values.
Ground answers in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not teach + or * here — those are later units.
Assume unit 1 (print + new line) is done; do not re-teach it in depth.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching unit 2 of Python printing. Advance only once the learner can predict that commas print values in order with one space between them, mixing text and numbers freely.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Commas print multiple values
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: You can pass several values to print() separated by commas, and it prints them in order. Python automatically puts a single space between each value. For example, print("Score:", 100) prints Score: 100.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Commas mix text and numbers
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Commas happily combine text and numbers without any conversion. print("Age:", 25) works directly — you do not need to turn the number into text first. This makes commas the easiest way to print a label next to a value.

questions.answer: Score: 100 — the comma prints the values in order with a single space between them.

hints.text: Commas add one space between values.

questions.prompt: Do you need to convert the number in print("Age:", 25) before printing it?
options: No, commas handle mixed text and numbers
questions.answer: No, commas handle mixed text and numbers

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting the comma version to print with no space between values.
commonMistakes.correction: The comma automatically inserts one space between values. If you need no space, that is what + (next-but-one unit) is for.

units.title: Joining Strings with + and Converting Numbers with str()
units.goal: Join strings with + and correctly include a number by converting it with str().

teacherBrain.persona: A friendly Python instructor who teaches by predicting output together.
objectives: Have the learner join text with + and fix a string+number error using str().
guidelines: Show print("Hello, " + "world") first, then the failing string+number case.
Introduce str() as the fix, and mention commas remain an easy alternative.
Ground answers in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not teach * here — that is the next unit.
Keep to + and str(); assume commas (unit 2) are known.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching unit 3 of Python printing. Advance only once the learner can explain that + joins strings and that a number must be wrapped in str() to join it to text. If they try "Age: " + 30, stop and show the str() fix.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: + joins strings
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: The + operator joins (concatenates) two strings into one, with nothing added between them. print("Hello, " + "world") prints Hello, world. Unlike commas, + does not insert a space, so you add spaces yourself inside the quotes.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Convert numbers with str()
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: You cannot join a string and a number with +; Python raises a TypeError. Convert the number to text first with str(): print("Age: " + str(25)) prints Age: 25. (A comma, like print("Age:", 25), avoids the conversion entirely.)

questions.prompt: Why does print("Age: " + 30) cause an error, and how do you fix it with +?
questions.answer: Because + cannot join a string and a number (TypeError). Fix it by converting the number: print("Age: " + str(30)).

hints.text: How do you turn a number into text?

questions.answer: Hello, world — + joins the two strings with no extra space added.

hints.text: + glues strings exactly as written, including the space you typed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using + to join a string and a number, e.g. "Age: " + 30.
commonMistakes.correction: That is a TypeError. Convert the number with str(30), or use a comma: print("Age:", 30).

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting + to add a space between the joined strings.
commonMistakes.correction: + adds nothing between strings; include the space yourself inside the quotes, e.g. "Hello, " + "world".

units.title: Repeating Strings with *
units.goal: Repeat a string a given number of times with the * operator.

teacherBrain.persona: A friendly Python instructor who teaches by predicting output together.
objectives: Have the learner repeat a string with * and predict the result.
guidelines: Show print("ab" * 3) and print("=" * 10) and ask what they print.
Note * repeats with no spaces added; contrast briefly with * between numbers (multiply).
Ground answers in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not re-teach + or commas in depth; assume earlier units are done.
Do not teach f-strings or loops.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching unit 4 of Python printing. Advance only once the learner can predict that "ab" * 3 is ababab (no spaces) and knows * between two numbers multiplies.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: * repeats a string
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: The * operator repeats a string a given number of times, with nothing added between copies. print("ab" * 3) prints ababab, and print("=" * 10) prints ==========. This is handy for drawing simple separators.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: * between numbers multiplies
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Between two numbers, * is ordinary multiplication: print(4 * 3) prints 12. So * repeats when one side is a string, and multiplies when both sides are numbers.

hints.text: * repeats the string, adding no spaces.

questions.prompt: What does print(4 * 3) print, and why is it different from repeating a string?
questions.answer: 12 — between two numbers * multiplies, whereas with a string one side it repeats.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting "ab" * 3 to add spaces, e.g. 'ab ab ab'.
commonMistakes.correction: * repeats with no separator: "ab" * 3 is ababab.
